Oscilloscopes and logic analyzers are used to debug timing problems in interrupt handlers and serial communication. Laboratory companion to EENG-3085.

Packet-switched network architecture is examined layer by layer, from framing and medium access control up through routing and basic transport protocols, using layered reference models to organize the material. Queueing delay, throughput, and error control are analyzed quantitatively for simple network topologies. Case studies cover wired local area networks and wireless access, contrasting their medium access and error-handling strategies.

DC, induction, and synchronous machines are analyzed through equivalent circuit models that predict torque, speed, and efficiency under varying load, and the course extends this to the power electronic drives that control them. Steady-state and basic dynamic behavior are covered for each machine type, along with the switching converter topologies commonly paired with them. Worked problems size a motor and drive combination for a target speed and torque profile.

Students run induction and DC machines on a test bench, measuring torque-speed curves with a dynamometer and comparing them to the equivalent circuit predictions developed in lecture. A later session connects a machine to a variable-frequency drive and records startup and speed-regulation behavior under changing load. Laboratory companion to EENG-3100.

Manufacturing lines are modeled as networks of workstations, buffers, and material flows, and the course covers throughput analysis, bottleneck identification, and scheduling techniques used to improve production system performance. Queueing and simulation models are applied to case studies such as a circuit-board assembly line or an electronics test station. Students build a simplified simulation of a production line and use it to evaluate proposed changes in staffing or buffer sizing. Cross-listed with MANU-4035.

Robot design is approached from the mechanism up: actuator selection and sizing, gear trains, manipulator kinematics, and the structural and electromechanical tradeoffs involved in building a physical robot rather than simulating one. Forward and inverse kinematics are developed for simple serial-link arms and applied to trajectory planning for a manipulator. The course emphasizes the mechanical and electromechanical design decisions that precede the navigation and perception algorithms covered in a separate robotics course.

Teams design, build, and program a robotic mechanism, integrating motors, sensors, and a microcontroller into a working system that must complete a specified physical task, such as picking up an object or navigating an obstacle course. Iterative testing and mechanical rework are a core part of the course, with students expected to diagnose and fix hardware failures under time pressure. Laboratory companion to EENG-3115.

Transduction mechanisms for common sensors, resistive, capacitive, and photonic, are covered alongside the signal-conditioning circuitry needed to turn a small sensor output into a usable measurement: instrumentation amplifiers, bridge circuits, and filtering for noise rejection. Error sources such as drift, nonlinearity, and electromagnetic interference are analyzed with an eye toward practical measurement system design. Case studies cover strain measurement, temperature sensing, and optical detection.

Signal-conditioning circuits for common sensors such as strain gauges, thermistors, and photodiodes are built and characterized here, with students measuring sensitivity and noise floor against datasheet specifications. A final exercise integrates a sensor, conditioning circuit, and simple readout display into a working measurement instrument. Laboratory companion to EENG-3125.

Electromagnetic field quantities such as electric field strength, transmission-line standing-wave ratio, and waveguide propagation characteristics are measured here using a network analyzer and probe setups, with results compared to the analytical predictions from lecture. A final exercise characterizes a transmission-line or waveguide section and extracts its propagation constant from measured data. Laboratory companion to EENG-3010.

Student teams select and scope a substantial electrical engineering design project, then carry it from a written requirements specification through a system-level architecture and a detailed subsystem design. Teams document design tradeoffs, build early breadboard or simulation prototypes of critical subsystems, and defend their approach at a formal design review. The term ends with a written proposal report and an oral presentation to a faculty panel.

Teams carry their proposed design into full construction, integrating subsystems into a working prototype and debugging interactions that only appear once the whole system runs together. Formal test plans verify the prototype against the original requirements, and results drive a final round of design changes. The course closes with a written final report and a public oral demonstration of the finished project.

Disordered semiconductors such as amorphous silicon and chalcogenide glasses depart from the periodic lattice assumptions of standard device theory, and this course builds the physical picture needed to understand them: band tails, localized states, and variable-range hopping transport. Students compare density-of-states models against transport measurements and connect the physics to thin-film transistors, photovoltaic cells, and memory switching devices. Problem sets emphasize order-of-magnitude estimation over closed-form solutions, since amorphous materials rarely offer one.

Semiconductor device behavior is derived from the drift-diffusion and continuity equations, moving beyond simplified band-and-junction models to capture short-channel effects, velocity saturation, and other second-order behavior in modern field-effect transistors. Bipolar transistor high-frequency limitations and heterojunction devices are also examined. Students use numerical device simulation to explore behavior that lacks a convenient closed-form solution.

Microelectromechanical sensors and actuators are treated as complete systems: a pressure sensor, an accelerometer, or a micromirror is studied from its mechanical structure through the electronics that read or drive it. The course surveys common transduction mechanisms, capacitive, piezoresistive, and piezoelectric, and shows how each couples to signal-conditioning circuitry. Fabrication detail is kept at a conceptual level throughout, with the emphasis placed on system-level integration and performance.

Students characterize packaged microsystem devices such as accelerometers and pressure sensors on the bench, measuring sensitivity, offset, and noise and building the signal-conditioning circuitry needed to read them out. Later sessions introduce a microfabricated test structure and ask students to relate its measured mechanical response to its design geometry. Laboratory companion to EENG-4025.

Manufacturing defects in digital circuits are modeled as stuck-at and bridging faults, and the course develops automatic test pattern generation techniques to detect them, including path sensitization and fault simulation. Design-for-testability structures such as scan chains and built-in self-test are covered alongside the tradeoffs they impose on chip area and speed. Homework problems have students generate test vectors by hand for small combinational circuits before moving to tool-assisted methods.

Static gate design expands here into dynamic logic families, memory circuits including SRAM and DRAM cell structures, and clocking and timing issues such as clock skew and setup and hold margins. Low-power design techniques, including voltage scaling and clock gating, are introduced alongside their tradeoffs against speed and reliability. Students analyze and design circuits that go well beyond simple static gates.

Students design and simulate the dynamic logic and memory circuits introduced in lecture, laying out an SRAM cell or a dynamic gate and verifying its read and write margins through transistor-level simulation. A semester project integrates a small memory block or a low-power logic circuit and evaluates it against area, speed, and power targets. Laboratory companion to EENG-4040.

Digital integrated circuits are examined at the chip level here, covering interconnect resistance and capacitance modeling, signal integrity issues such as crosstalk and ground bounce, and the power distribution networks needed to deliver clean supply voltage across a large die. Input and output buffer design and electrostatic discharge protection are covered as the interface between a chip and the outside world. The course complements gate-level design courses by focusing on effects that only appear at full-chip scale.

Microwave circuits built from solid-state devices are analyzed using scattering parameters, covering transistor amplifier design for gain and stability, oscillator topologies, and mixer circuits used in microwave transceivers. Impedance matching networks are designed graphically to meet gain, bandwidth, and noise-figure targets. Design examples work through a complete low-noise amplifier or oscillator from device selection to matching network layout.

This course extends the fundamentals of laser operation into pulsed and high-power regimes, covering Q-switching, mode-locking, and gain-switching techniques used to generate short optical pulses. Nonlinear effects such as harmonic generation and their role in extending laser wavelength coverage are also examined. Design problems estimate pulse energy, peak power, and repetition rate for a specified laser configuration.

A pulsed or Q-switched laser system is operated on the bench here, with students measuring pulse energy, duration, and beam quality and comparing results to the mode-locking and Q-switching theory covered in lecture. A characterization exercise records output power as a function of pump level to extract threshold and slope efficiency for the system under test. Laboratory companion to EENG-4060.

The electro-optic effect, the change in a materials refractive index under an applied electric field, is developed from crystal symmetry arguments and applied to the design of optical modulators and switches built in semiconductor and electro-optic crystal platforms. Phase and amplitude modulation schemes are analyzed for bandwidth and drive-voltage requirements. The course treats electro-optic modulation as a distinct device class from the light-emitting and light-detecting devices covered in earlier optoelectronics courses.

Surface plasmon polaritons, the coupled oscillations of free electrons and light at a metal-dielectric interface, are developed from Maxwells equations and used to explain field confinement below the diffraction limit. Applications covered include plasmonic waveguides, sensors that exploit the sensitivity of surface plasmon resonance to a local refractive index change, and enhanced light-matter interaction in nanostructured metals. Numerical examples estimate propagation length and confinement for representative metal-dielectric geometries.

Ionized gases are described through single-particle motion in electric and magnetic fields, then through fluid and kinetic models that predict collective behavior such as Debye shielding, plasma oscillations, and wave propagation. Diagnostic techniques used to measure plasma parameters, including probes and spectroscopic methods, are covered alongside the theory they are meant to test. Applications span fusion confinement concepts, plasma processing, and space plasma phenomena. Cross-listed with NUCL-3055.

Working with a small laboratory plasma source, students measure electron temperature and density using electrostatic probes and observe basic plasma phenomena such as sheath formation and wave propagation. Diagnostic techniques including optical emission spectroscopy are used to characterize discharge conditions, and results are compared to the theoretical models covered in lecture. Laboratory companion to EENG-4080. Cross-listed with NUCL-3060.

Radiation from current distributions is derived from first principles here, starting with the elementary dipole and building through gain, directivity, and polarization to array factor calculations for linear arrays. Design exercises ask students to size a dipole or patch element for a target frequency and input impedance, then verify the result against a simulated radiation pattern. The course treats antennas as a design problem in electromagnetics rather than a component chosen from a catalog.

Building on discrete-time system theory, this course focuses on designing filters to meet a target specification and implementing them under real hardware constraints such as fixed-point arithmetic, limited word length, and finite processor throughput. Filter design methods including windowing and equiripple approximation are compared for how closely they meet passband and stopband requirements. Students translate a filter specification into a working implementation and verify it against the target frequency response.

Filters designed in lecture are implemented on a signal-processing platform, with students measuring frequency response and quantifying the error introduced by fixed-point rounding relative to a floating-point reference. A closing project applies a designed filter to a recorded signal and evaluates whether it meets its passband and stopband targets. Laboratory companion to EENG-4095.

Continuous-time control designs are adapted for implementation on a microcontroller here, covering sampling rate selection, discretization of a continuous controller, and the effects of quantization and computational delay on closed-loop stability. Proportional-integral-derivative controllers are implemented in fixed-point arithmetic and evaluated against the same performance metrics used for their continuous counterparts. The course bridges classical control theory and the realities of running a controller on limited embedded hardware.

A microcontroller running a digital control algorithm is used to regulate a physical plant, such as a motor speed or a temperature loop, and students tune the controller on hardware and compare its response to the simulation from lecture. Data logging and real-time plotting are used to diagnose steady-state error and oscillation caused by sampling rate or quantization. Laboratory companion to EENG-4105.

Mobile robot navigation is built up from kinematic models of wheeled platforms through sensor fusion, localization, and path planning algorithms, connecting each topic to the perception and control problems a robot must solve to move through an environment. Coverage includes basic mapping techniques and obstacle avoidance strategies evaluated in simulation before any hardware is involved. Students implement a simplified planning algorithm and test it against a set of simulated environments.

Wheeled robot platforms are programmed here to execute the localization and path-planning algorithms introduced in lecture, using onboard sensors such as encoders and rangefinders to navigate a marked course. Teams iterate on a semester project that must complete a navigation task with a fixed budget of sensors and computation. Laboratory companion to EENG-4115.

Radio signal behavior over real terrain and buildings is modeled beyond simple free-space propagation, covering reflection, diffraction, and scattering mechanisms and the empirical and statistical models used to predict path loss in practice. Multipath fading, shadowing, and Doppler spread are analyzed for their effect on link reliability. Link budget calculations tie the propagation models to overall system range and coverage planning.

Field and bench measurements here characterize how radio signals attenuate and fade over distance, comparing measured path loss to free-space and empirical propagation models covered in lecture. Students also measure multipath effects indoors using a network analyzer and relate the results to fading statistics. Laboratory companion to EENG-4125.

Digital control design is developed from the z-transform through pulse transfer functions, covering discretization of continuous plants, digital compensator design, and stability analysis on the z-plane. State-space methods for digital controllers, including pole placement and observer design, extend the classical transform-based techniques covered earlier in the course. Design examples apply these methods to mechanical and electromechanical plants such as a positioning stage or a motor drive. Cross-listed with MECH-4025.

Patentability, novelty, and obviousness are introduced from an engineer's perspective, covering how to read a patent claim, search prior art, and document an invention disclosure in a way that supports a later patent application. Case studies drawn from electrical and electronic technologies illustrate how claims are drafted to cover a range of implementations. The course is designed for engineers who will work alongside intellectual property professionals rather than for those pursuing formal legal training.

An entry point to product design, covering engineering sketching, dimensioning, and basic tolerancing alongside an overview of core manufacturing processes such as casting, injection molding, and machining. Simple design-for-manufacture guidelines introduce how part geometry and material choice affect cost and producibility. Weekly design exercises build toward a small manufactured component completed in the paired laboratory.

The lab pairs basic machine shop practice (mill, lathe, drill press, and hand tools) with measurement technique using calipers, micrometers, and dial indicators. Students fabricate a sequence of simple parts from engineering drawings, checking dimensions and tolerances against spec, and submit lab reports documenting process choices and results. Safety procedures and shop etiquette are enforced from the first session. Laboratory companion to MANU-1005.

Material selection is framed as a design decision: given a set of functional requirements, students use property charts and selection indices to weigh candidate metals, polymers, ceramics, and composites against cost, weight, and manufacturability. Short case studies trace historical material substitutions, such as aluminum for steel in automotive panels, to show how selection criteria shift with application. Cross-listed with MATL-3010.

Design work advances to parametric CAD modeling, geometric dimensioning and tolerancing, and formal design-for-manufacture and design-for-assembly review. Process planning introduces CNC machining sequences and fixturing strategy for mid-complexity parts, with tolerance stack-up analysis used to catch fit problems before they reach the shop floor. A term project carries a component from concept sketch through a manufacturing-ready drawing package.

Building on first-year shop skills, this lab moves to CNC milling and turning, with students programming toolpaths from CAD models and verifying dimensional accuracy against tolerance stacks. Teams assemble multi-part subsystems, troubleshoot fit and function issues, and document machining parameters and iteration history in structured reports. Laboratory companion to MANU-2010.

Conventional machining processes such as turning, milling, drilling, and grinding are analyzed through cutting mechanics: chip formation, tool geometry, and the speeds and feeds that govern material removal rate. Tool wear mechanisms and their effect on surface finish and dimensional accuracy are covered alongside selection of cutting tool materials such as carbide and ceramic inserts. Cross-listed with MECH-3055.

Design work matures toward production readiness: students develop a manufacturing process plan for a multi-part assembly, estimate unit cost across candidate processes, and specify tooling requirements for a target production volume. Simulation tools check assembly tolerances and manufacturability before committing to hard tooling. The course bridges the single-part focus of earlier design courses with the system-level view needed for the capstone.

Statistical methods for monitoring and improving process quality open with control charts: X-bar and R charts, p-charts, and the rules used to detect an out-of-control process. Process capability indices such as Cp and Cpk quantify how well a process meets specification limits, and acceptance sampling plans are introduced for incoming inspection. Worked examples draw on measurement data from machined parts and assembly lines. Cross-listed with MECH-3060.

This lab puts control-chart theory into practice on the measurement floor. Students run gauge repeatability and reproducibility studies, calibrate calipers, micrometers, and coordinate measuring machines, and build X-bar and R charts from real part measurements. Teams sample a running process, compute Cp and Cpk from their own data, and flag when a process drifts out of control. Reports document measurement system error alongside the quality decisions it drives. Laboratory companion to MANU-3010.

Laboratory sessions pair mechanical testing (tensile, hardness, and impact) with failure analysis of fractured or corroded samples, building the evidence base for a term-long material selection project. Students benchmark candidate materials against a design brief, document test procedures and data in formal reports, and present a final material recommendation. Laboratory companion to MANU-2005. Cross-listed with MATL-3015.

Fiber-reinforced composites are introduced through their constituent phases: reinforcing fibers such as glass and carbon, and polymer, metal, or ceramic matrices that bind them. Coverage includes laminate stacking sequences, basic micromechanics for predicting stiffness and strength, and common fabrication routes like hand layup, filament winding, and resin transfer molding. Case studies from aerospace and automotive panels illustrate how fiber orientation and matrix choice drive performance tradeoffs. Cross-listed with MATL-3055.

Design-for-manufacture rules are examined process by process: draft angles and wall thickness for injection molding, bend allowances and minimum flange lengths for sheet metal, and parting-line placement for casting. Students redesign a supplied part to reduce cycle time or scrap rate under a named manufacturing process, then justify the cost impact of each change. Cross-listed with MECH-3050.

Coverage spans the equipment and layout decisions behind moving materials through a factory or warehouse: conveyors, automated guided vehicles, forklifts, and storage racking. Students learn to size throughput requirements, lay out receiving and staging areas, and calculate basic queuing and buffer capacity for a production line. Case examples cover distribution centers and assembly plants alike.

Lean principles built around waste elimination and flow are applied across both factory floors and service operations. Tools covered include value stream mapping, kanban pull systems, 5S workplace organization, and single-minute exchange of die for reducing changeover time. Students map an existing process, identify non-value-added steps, and propose a redesigned workflow with supporting metrics.

Production planning and inventory management are formalized through models such as economic order quantity, safety stock calculation, and material requirements planning. Students build a master production schedule from a forecasted demand pattern and translate it into a time-phased materials plan for a multi-level bill of materials. Forecasting error and its effect on inventory buffers is examined through sensitivity analysis.

The first half of the senior capstone carries a product from an initial concept through a validated design ready for build. Teams define requirements, iterate through concept selection and detailed design, and produce a manufacturing process plan with supplier and tooling commitments in place. The term concludes with a design review and a build plan that carries directly into the second capstone term.

The second half of the senior capstone executes the build plan set in the first term. Teams procure parts, coordinate shop and supplier schedules, and assemble a functional working prototype from their own design package. Testing against the original requirements drives a final round of design changes and troubleshooting. The term ends with a working prototype demonstration and a written design history documenting decisions and tradeoffs across both terms.

Location decisions for manufacturing capacity are analyzed against labor cost, logistics distance, tariff exposure, and quality risk across regions. Case studies of multinational producers illustrate tradeoffs between offshoring, nearshoring, and reshoring, including the hidden costs of extended supply chains such as inventory buffers and quality escapes. Students build a landed-cost comparison for a candidate product across two or more manufacturing locations. Cross-listed with MECH-4045.

Automated manufacturing equipment is built from the integration of sensors, actuators, and embedded control, and this course covers PLC programming, servo motor control, and sensor selection for closed-loop feedback. Students design and program a control system for a small automated workcell, such as a pick-and-place station or a robotic dispensing arm, addressing timing, safety interlocks, and fault handling. Cross-listed with MECH-4040.

Numerical optimization techniques such as gradient-based search, genetic algorithms, and topology optimization are applied to structural and mechanical design problems with competing objectives like weight, stiffness, and cost. Students formulate design variables, constraints, and objective functions for case problems such as bracket redesign or truss layout, then solve them with optimization software. Cross-listed with MECH-4030.

Cyclic loading and its effect on mechanical components anchors this course: S-N curves, stress concentration factors, and mean-stress corrections are used to predict fatigue life for shafts, fasteners, and welded joints. Crack initiation and propagation are introduced through basic fracture mechanics, including crack growth rate models. Historical failures, from aircraft fuselages to bridge components, illustrate how design margins are set in practice. Cross-listed with MECH-4035.

Manufacturing lines are modeled as networks of workstations, buffers, and material flows, and the course covers throughput analysis, bottleneck identification, and scheduling techniques used to improve production system performance. Queueing and simulation models are applied to case studies such as a circuit-board assembly line or an electronics test station. Students build a simplified simulation of a production line and use it to evaluate proposed changes in staffing or buffer sizing. Cross-listed with EENG-3110.

Sequencing and scheduling problems are formulated for both job shop and flow shop environments, covering dispatching rules, critical ratio scheduling, and bottleneck-focused approaches such as drum-buffer-rope. Students compare heuristic scheduling rules against optimal solutions for small problem instances and evaluate tradeoffs between makespan, tardiness, and machine utilization. A term assignment schedules a multi-product production run under capacity constraints.

Building past the control-chart foundation of introductory quality control, this course covers design of experiments for process optimization, multivariate and EWMA control charts for detecting subtle shifts, and regression-based methods for relating process inputs to output quality. The DMAIC framework structures a term-long improvement project on a real or simulated process. Emphasis falls on situations where single-variable charts miss interacting effects.

An independent study format lets a student pursue an open design problem under faculty supervision, beginning with a written proposal that scopes the problem, deliverables, and schedule. Work proceeds through concept development, analysis, and design iteration appropriate to the chosen topic, culminating in a final written report and an oral presentation to faculty. Cross-listed with MATL-4035.

Manufacturers face volatile input costs, and this course examines how futures, forwards, options, and swaps are used to hedge exposure to raw-material prices, energy costs, and currency movements. Students build hedge ratios for a commodity-exposed production plan, evaluate basis risk, and compare exchange-traded contracts against over-the-counter alternatives. Applications draw on metals, plastics resin, and energy markets relevant to a manufacturing supply chain.

Fabrication and assembly methods for ships and offshore structures are covered, including hull plate forming, block construction sequencing, and welding procedures suited to marine-grade steel. Corrosion protection strategies such as cathodic protection and coating systems address the demands of a saltwater environment. Case studies examine how large sub-assemblies are built in modules and joined at final erection.

A team project embeds students directly with an industrial partner's operations to study a live production or logistics problem on-site. Teams scope the problem with the partner, gather operational data, and develop process or system recommendations grounded in the partner's actual constraints. The term concludes with a written report and a presentation delivered to the partner organization.

A broad survey introduces the four major materials classes (metals, polymers, ceramics, and composites) alongside the manufacturing processes commonly paired with each, such as casting for metals and injection molding for polymers. Basic property concepts, including strength, stiffness, and ductility, are related to atomic and molecular structure at a qualitative level. The course sets up the material and process vocabulary used throughout both the Materials Science and Manufacturing programs.

Material properties are derived from underlying physics: atomic bonding types, crystal structure, and electron band theory explain why some solids conduct electricity and others insulate. Thermal and magnetic properties, including heat capacity and basic ferromagnetism, are connected back to the same structural and electronic framework. Problem sets emphasize quantitative prediction of property trends across material families.

Structure-property relationships across metals, ceramics, and polymers are developed through mechanical testing, phase diagrams, and the microstructural features that control strength and toughness, including grain size, phase fraction, and defect density. Students interpret binary phase diagrams to predict microstructure from processing history and relate that microstructure to measured mechanical properties. The course applies these relationships to selecting materials for representative engineering components.

Gibbs free energy, chemical potential, and phase equilibria form the thermodynamic framework used to predict which phases are stable at a given temperature and composition. Students construct binary phase diagrams from thermodynamic data and interpret them to identify equilibrium phases, tie lines, and invariant reactions. Reaction equilibria and basic electrochemical concepts introduce the driving forces behind oxidation and related degradation processes. Problem sets connect thermodynamic calculations to the phase diagrams used across materials selection and processing.

Ficks laws, Arrhenius-type rate expressions, and time-temperature-transformation diagrams describe how atoms move through solids and how that motion drives phase change. Applications include predicting carburizing depth in heat-treated steel, solidification rate effects on grain structure, and nucleation and growth in diffusion-controlled transformations. Problem sets require solving transport equations under specified boundary conditions and reading TTT and CCT diagrams to predict the resulting microstructure.

Laboratory sessions put students on X-ray diffractometers and spectroscopy instruments to collect data on unknown material samples, then walk through pattern matching and quantitative analysis to identify phases and composition. Each session culminates in a written report defending an identification against the collected data. Instrument calibration and sample preparation practices are emphasized throughout. Laboratory companion to MATL-3025.

Material selection is framed as a design decision: given a set of functional requirements, students use property charts and selection indices to weigh candidate metals, polymers, ceramics, and composites against cost, weight, and manufacturability. Short case studies trace historical material substitutions, such as aluminum for steel in automotive panels, to show how selection criteria shift with application. Cross-listed with MANU-2005.

Laboratory sessions pair mechanical testing (tensile, hardness, and impact) with failure analysis of fractured or corroded samples, building the evidence base for a term-long material selection project. Students benchmark candidate materials against a design brief, document test procedures and data in formal reports, and present a final material recommendation. Laboratory companion to MATL-3010. Cross-listed with MANU-3020.

Crystal systems, Bravais lattices, and common structures such as FCC, BCC, and HCP are built up systematically and used to index planes and directions with Miller notation. Point defects, dislocations, and grain boundaries are introduced as departures from perfect crystal structure that govern later property discussions. Diffraction geometry, including Braggs law, connects crystal structure to the patterns collected in later characterization work. Exercises have students construct unit cells and compute planar and linear densities by hand.

X-ray diffraction, energy-dispersive spectroscopy, and surface-sensitive methods are used to quantify composition and crystal structure in unknown samples. Diffraction patterns are indexed against reference data to identify phases, while spectra are used for elemental analysis of metals, ceramics, and thin films. Students apply these techniques to materials identification problems drawn from failure analysis and quality control contexts.

The physics of electron-sample interaction underlies this study of electron microscopy, covering electron generation, lens systems, and imaging modes such as secondary electron, backscattered electron, and diffraction contrast. Resolution limits and specimen preparation constraints are compared across scanning and transmission instruments, with attention to how each mode reveals different microstructural features. Students learn to select an imaging mode and detector configuration appropriate to a given specimen and question.

Hands-on sessions cover sample preparation, mounting, and coating techniques, followed by operation of a scanning electron microscope to capture and interpret micrographs of metal, ceramic, and polymer specimens. Basic diffraction patterns are collected and indexed to identify crystal structure. Each session produces a written report pairing imaging results with microstructural interpretation. Laboratory companion to MATL-3030.

Elastic and plastic deformation of engineering metals and polymers is examined through stress-strain testing, yield criteria, and strain hardening models. Students study fatigue crack initiation and growth, creep at elevated temperature, and fracture mechanics parameters used to predict failure. Case studies connect microstructure to macroscopic mechanical response across a range of material classes. Cross-listed with MECH-3030.

Metallic alloys are examined through the phase transformations and strengthening mechanisms that define their mechanical behavior: precipitation hardening, solid solution strengthening, grain refinement, and martensitic transformation in steels. Heat treatment schedules are designed and predicted using time-temperature-transformation and continuous-cooling-transformation diagrams for specific alloy systems. Case studies cover aluminum aerospace alloys and hardened tool steels.

Ceramic materials are introduced through their crystal structures, ionic and covalent bonding, and the processing routes used to form dense parts, including powder pressing, sintering, and firing. Mechanical behavior emphasizes brittle fracture and the flaw sensitivity that distinguishes ceramics from metals, alongside thermal properties relevant to refractory and electronic applications. Examples range from structural alumina components to piezoelectric ceramics.

Fiber-reinforced composites are introduced through their constituent phases: reinforcing fibers such as glass and carbon, and polymer, metal, or ceramic matrices that bind them. Coverage includes laminate stacking sequences, basic micromechanics for predicting stiffness and strength, and common fabrication routes like hand layup, filament winding, and resin transfer molding. Case studies from aerospace and automotive panels illustrate how fiber orientation and matrix choice drive performance tradeoffs. Cross-listed with MANU-3025.

Polymer chain architecture, molecular weight distribution, and crystallinity are connected to processing behavior across thermoplastics, thermosets, and elastomers. Processing methods such as extrusion, injection molding, and compression molding are examined alongside the viscoelastic response that distinguishes polymers from metals and ceramics, including creep, stress relaxation, and rate-dependent stiffness. Applications span commodity packaging plastics to engineering polymers used in structural components.

Covers the physical behavior of polymeric materials: chain conformation and molecular weight distribution, glass transition and crystallization, viscoelasticity, and the rheological measurements used to characterize melt and solution behavior. Problem sets connect molecular structure to bulk mechanical and thermal properties observed in processing. The course serves both chemical engineering and materials students, reflected in its dual listing. Cross-listed with CHEM-3035.

Electrochemical half-reactions and Pourbaix diagrams explain why metals corrode in specific environments and how passivation can slow or stop attack. Uniform, galvanic, pitting, and crevice corrosion are distinguished by mechanism and by the inspection evidence each leaves behind. Oxidation of metals at elevated temperature is treated alongside aqueous corrosion, with an emphasis on protective coatings and cathodic protection as mitigation strategies. Case examples span pipelines, marine hardware, and high-temperature alloy components.

Teams scope a materials engineering project from an open-ended problem statement, defining functional requirements, constraints, and success criteria before any material is selected. Concept generation and down-selection draw on property charts, selection indices, and cost and manufacturability screens developed in earlier design coursework. Each team produces a design proposal, a test plan, and a project schedule that carries into the second semester of the sequence. Progress is documented through periodic design reviews.

Teams execute the test and evaluation plan defined in the first semester, building or sourcing prototype hardware and characterizing it against the original design requirements. Design iterations respond to test data, with tradeoffs documented and justified against cost, performance, and manufacturability constraints. The sequence concludes with a final written report and a formal oral presentation defending the team's design decisions to a faculty panel. Lessons learned are captured for future project teams.

Linear elastic fracture mechanics introduces stress intensity factors and fracture toughness as the properties that govern crack growth in brittle and quasi-brittle materials. S-N curves and Paris law crack growth rates describe how cyclic loading accumulates damage well below a materials static strength. Case studies drawn from aerospace and pressure vessel failures connect fractographic evidence to the loading history that produced it. Students calculate critical crack size and estimate remaining fatigue life for a given component and load spectrum.

Band theory is extended from an introductory treatment to explain conductors, semiconductors, and insulators in quantitative terms, including doping, carrier concentration, and junction behavior. Dielectric response, ferroelectricity, and piezoelectricity are covered alongside diamagnetism, paramagnetism, and ferromagnetism as structure-dependent electronic and magnetic phenomena. Applications include sensors, capacitors, and magnetic storage media. Problem sets connect crystal structure and bonding to measured electrical and magnetic property data.

Metals, ceramics, polymers, and composites are evaluated against the added constraints of a biological environment: biocompatibility, degradation in vivo, and the foreign body response. Coverage includes titanium and cobalt-chromium alloys for implants, bioceramics and bioactive glasses, and resorbable polymers used in sutures and drug delivery. Sterilization methods and regulatory testing frameworks are introduced as constraints on material and process selection. Case studies cover joint replacements, stents, and tissue scaffolds.

Failed components are examined through a structured investigation sequence: visual inspection, fractography, metallography, and chemical analysis are combined to build a case for the root cause of failure. Common failure modes, including fatigue, overload, corrosion, and creep, are distinguished by the physical evidence each leaves on a fracture surface. Students practice writing a failure analysis report that ties observed evidence to a defensible root cause and a corrective action recommendation. Case studies span automotive, aerospace, and infrastructure components.

An independent study format lets a student pursue an open design problem under faculty supervision, beginning with a written proposal that scopes the problem, deliverables, and schedule. Work proceeds through concept development, analysis, and design iteration appropriate to the chosen topic, culminating in a final written report and an oral presentation to faculty. Cross-listed with MANU-4050.

Stress, strain, and the relationship between them under Hooke's law form the foundation of this course, applied first to axially loaded bars and then to circular shafts under torsion. Students compute deformation, factor of safety, and stress concentration in simple structural members. The course sets up the vocabulary and free body methods used throughout later mechanics coursework.

Newtonian mechanics of particles and rigid bodies grounds this course, covering position, velocity, and acceleration in rotating and translating reference frames. Students apply force-mass-acceleration and work-energy methods to problems in linkages, gears, and simple mechanisms, then extend the same tools to impulse and momentum. Rigid body rotation about fixed axes and general plane motion round out the semester's problem sets.

The first and second laws of thermodynamics anchor this course, developed through property tables, the ideal gas model, and control volume energy balances. Students evaluate work and heat transfer in closed and open systems, then apply the concepts to simple power and refrigeration cycles. Entropy generation and the limits it places on cycle efficiency close out the semester.

Bending, shear, and deflection of beams under distributed and concentrated loads extend the axial and torsional analysis introduced in earlier coursework. Students construct shear and moment diagrams, compute deflections by integration and superposition, and evaluate buckling of columns under compressive load. Combined loading problems and Mohr's circle for plane stress bring the semester's methods together for design against yield and instability.

Beams, shafts, and columns come off the whiteboard and onto the test frame in this laboratory. Students mount strain gauges and extensometers to measure bending and torsional deflection, then compare measured strain fields against the analytical predictions from lecture. Tension and buckling tests on standard specimens round out the semester, with each experiment closing in a written report that weighs measurement uncertainty against theory. Laboratory companion to MECH-2020.

Fluid statics and the control volume forms of mass, momentum, and energy conservation open this introduction to fluid mechanics, applied to problems in pipes, tanks, and open channels. Students use Bernoulli's equation and dimensional analysis to size simple flow systems and estimate friction losses in laminar and turbulent pipe flow. Lecture problems draw on manometry, flow measurement devices, and basic pump and turbine performance.

Pipe networks, venturi meters, and a small wind tunnel give this laboratory its hands-on core. Students measure head loss in laminar and turbulent pipe flow, calibrate flow meters against a reference standard, and characterize pump performance curves at varying speed. Each session ends with a report that reconciles measured data against the control volume methods developed in lecture. Laboratory companion to MECH-3005.

Conduction, convection, and radiation are treated as a unified set of energy transport mechanisms, beginning with steady and transient conduction in one and two dimensional geometries. Students size fins and extended surfaces, apply correlations for forced and natural convection, and compute radiative exchange between surfaces of varying geometry and emissivity. The course closes with heat exchanger analysis using the log mean temperature difference and effectiveness-NTU methods.

Free and forced response of single degree-of-freedom oscillators opens the course, with natural frequency, damping ratio, and resonance developed from spring-mass-damper models. Coverage extends to multi-degree-of-freedom systems, normal modes, and vibration isolation for rotating machinery. Problem sets emphasize predicting amplitude and frequency response from a system's physical parameters.

course_title: Modeling and Control of Dynamic Systems
course_desc: Differential equation models of mechanical, electrical, and electromechanical systems are converted into transfer functions and block diagrams as the starting point for this course. Students analyze first and second order system response to step and frequency inputs, then design basic proportional and PID feedback controllers. Root locus and Bode plot techniques are introduced as tools for predicting closed loop stability.

Elastic and plastic deformation of engineering metals and polymers is examined through stress-strain testing, yield criteria, and strain hardening models. Students study fatigue crack initiation and growth, creep at elevated temperature, and fracture mechanics parameters used to predict failure. Case studies connect microstructure to macroscopic mechanical response across a range of material classes. Cross-listed with MATL-3040.

Lagrangian and Hamiltonian formulations replace the vector Newtonian methods of introductory dynamics, providing a systematic route to the equations of motion for constrained multibody systems. Students derive equations for robotic linkages, vehicle suspensions, and other multi-link mechanisms, then implement numerical integration schemes to simulate their time response. Generalized coordinates, virtual work, and Lagrange multipliers for constraints are recurring tools throughout.

The Navier-Stokes equations are derived and solved for a set of classical exact solutions before the course turns to boundary layer theory and its role in drag prediction. Students analyze laminar to turbulent transition, separation, and wake formation over immersed bodies such as airfoils and cylinders. External flow problems involving lift and drag coefficients connect the theory to vehicle and structure design.

Ordinary and partial differential equations that arise in mechanical engineering problems are solved using series solutions, separation of variables, and Laplace transform methods. Students apply linear algebra and matrix methods to coupled systems of equations, then use numerical techniques including finite differences to approximate solutions that resist closed form treatment. Applications are drawn from vibration, heat conduction, and structural problems covered elsewhere in the curriculum.

Students redesign a supplied part to reduce cycle time or scrap rate under a named manufacturing process, then justify the cost impact of each change. Cross-listed with MANU-3030.

Cross-listed with MANU-2020.

Process capability indices such as Cp and Cpk quantify how well a process meets specification limits, and acceptance sampling plans are introduced for incoming inspection. Worked examples draw on measurement data from machined parts and assembly lines. Cross-listed with MANU-3010.

Teams identify a real mechanical engineering problem, write a requirements specification, and generate concept designs against competing criteria such as cost, manufacturability, and performance. Students run trade studies, build early prototypes or simulations to retire risk, and present a converged concept to a review panel. The course sets the technical and organizational foundation that carries into the build and test phase of the following semester.

Teams carry their approved concept from the prior semester into detailed design, fabrication, and testing. Students refine drawings and specifications, procure or machine components, and run a validation test plan against the original requirements. The course closes with a formal design review and a final report documenting what worked, what changed, and what the team would do differently.

Turbulence closure models, including eddy viscosity and Reynolds-averaged formulations, are developed alongside compressible gas dynamics for this advanced treatment of fluid flow. Students derive and apply the governing equations for shock waves, expansion fans, and choked flow in nozzles, then extend viscous flow theory to separated and three-dimensional boundary layers. The course is problem-set intensive, drawing on research-level fluid mechanics literature.

Blood flow through arteries, veins, and capillary beds is modeled using non-Newtonian viscosity relationships suited to biological tissue, with pulsatile flow and vessel compliance treated alongside classical fluid mechanics. Students also examine respiratory airflow through the branching airway tree and the fluid dynamics of implanted and external biomedical devices such as stents, valves, and dialysis equipment. Problem sets connect physiological measurements to fluid mechanical models of disease and device performance.

Digital control design is developed from the z-transform through pulse transfer functions, covering discretization of continuous plants, digital compensator design, and stability analysis on the z-plane. State-space methods for digital controllers, including pole placement and observer design, extend the classical transform-based techniques covered earlier in the course. Design examples apply these methods to mechanical and electromechanical plants such as a positioning stage or a motor drive. Cross-listed with EENG-4135.

Numerical optimization techniques such as gradient-based search, genetic algorithms, and topology optimization are applied to structural and mechanical design problems with competing objectives like weight, stiffness, and cost. Students formulate design variables, constraints, and objective functions for case problems such as bracket redesign or truss layout, then solve them with optimization software. Cross-listed with MANU-4025.

Cyclic loading and its effect on mechanical components anchors this course: S-N curves, stress concentration factors, and mean-stress corrections are used to predict fatigue life for shafts, fasteners, and welded joints. Crack initiation and propagation are introduced through basic fracture mechanics, including crack growth rate models. Historical failures, from aircraft fuselages to bridge components, illustrate how design margins are set in practice. Cross-listed with MANU-4030.

Automated manufacturing equipment is built from the integration of sensors, actuators, and embedded control, and this course covers PLC programming, servo motor control, and sensor selection for closed-loop feedback. Students design and program a control system for a small automated workcell, such as a pick-and-place station or a robotic dispensing arm, addressing timing, safety interlocks, and fault handling. Cross-listed with MANU-4020.

Location decisions for manufacturing capacity are analyzed against labor cost, logistics distance, tariff exposure, and quality risk across regions. Case studies of multinational producers illustrate tradeoffs between offshoring, nearshoring, and reshoring, including the hidden costs of extended supply chains such as inventory buffers and quality escapes. Students build a landed-cost comparison for a candidate product across two or more manufacturing locations. Cross-listed with MANU-4015.

Topics in this course rotate by offering and are announced in advance, drawing on emerging areas of mechanical engineering such as soft robotics, additive manufacturing process design, or biomechanical tissue modeling. Each offering is organized around a focused set of readings, problem sets, and a term project appropriate to the topic. The course allows the department to bring current research areas into the senior curriculum.

Fission physics, the nuclear fuel cycle, and the major reactor types in commercial use are surveyed in this broad overview of the nuclear engineering field. Students trace uranium from mining through enrichment, fuel fabrication, reactor use, and waste management, and examine the regulatory and safety framework governing each stage. The course is oriented toward giving incoming majors a map of the discipline before they specialize.

course_title: Nuclear Engineering and Radiological Sciences I
course_desc: Nuclear reactions, radioactive decay, and the interaction of radiation with matter form the shared foundation of nuclear engineering and radiological sciences covered in this course. Students calculate activity, half-life, and basic radiation dose, and survey reactor concepts alongside medical and industrial uses of radiation. The course establishes the vocabulary and calculation methods used throughout the rest of the curriculum.

course_title: Nuclear Engineering and Radiological Sciences II
course_desc: Building on the introductory survey, this course develops quantitative dose calculation methods, shielding fundamentals, and reactor physics concepts in greater depth. Students compute effective dose from mixed radiation fields and apply attenuation calculations to simple shielding geometries. The course bridges the department's introductory sequence and its more specialized upper-level coursework.

Coolant flow through reactor core channels is the organizing problem of this course, covering single-phase pressure drop, flow distribution among parallel channels, and the onset of boiling in two-phase conditions. Students apply mass, momentum, and energy balances to simplified core and heat exchanger geometries to predict coolant temperature and pressure profiles. The course builds the fluid mechanics foundation needed for later reactor thermal-hydraulics and safety analysis coursework.

Point kinetics equations describe how reactor power responds to changes in reactivity, and form the analytical center of this course. Students work through delayed neutron effects, reactivity feedback from temperature and void changes, and transient response to control rod motion or reactivity insertion accidents. Numerical solution of the kinetics equations is used throughout to predict power excursions and their time constants.

Reactor thermal hydraulics covers the heat generation, conduction, and removal processes that keep a reactor core within its safety limits. Students analyze fuel rod heat conduction, critical heat flux, and departure from nucleate boiling, and evaluate how coolant flow and pressure drop interact with core power distribution. Steady-state and transient safety margins are calculated for representative core geometries using standard correlations. The course connects core-level thermal design to the broader safety analysis performed for full reactor systems.

Students operate scintillation and semiconductor radiation detectors in this laboratory, calibrating energy response and characterizing counting statistics against theoretical distributions. Weekly experiments cover pulse height analysis, dead time correction, and background subtraction using standard nuclear instrumentation electronics. Each experiment concludes with a written report presenting measured data alongside its statistical uncertainty. Laboratory companion to NUCL-3025.

This laboratory puts the measurement techniques of its companion lecture into practice, with students calibrating detectors, counting certified sources, and performing efficiency and geometry corrections on their own data. Experiments cover gamma spectroscopy, alpha and beta counting, and simple neutron detection setups. Each session produces a written report documenting procedure, results, and measurement uncertainty. Laboratory companion to NUCL-3030.

Scintillation, semiconductor, and gas-filled detectors are compared for their response to radiation, energy resolution, and appropriate applications. Students study the electronics chain from preamplifier through pulse height analysis, and apply counting statistics to distinguish real signal from background and detector noise. Signal processing techniques for both pulse counting and spectroscopic measurement are covered.

Practical measurement techniques for gamma spectroscopy, alpha and beta counting, and neutron detection are developed for use in laboratory and field settings. Students calibrate instruments against certified sources, apply efficiency and geometry corrections, and evaluate measurement uncertainty for a range of detector types. Case studies cover environmental monitoring, contamination surveys, and material assay problems.

Nuclear materials examines how structural and cladding materials behave under the combined stress of high temperature, corrosive coolant chemistry, and intense radiation fields. Students study radiation-induced defects, swelling, and embrittlement in reactor vessel steels and cladding alloys, and evaluate material selection tradeoffs across different reactor concepts. Mechanical property changes over a component's service life are tracked using standard degradation models. The course builds the materials background needed for later fuel performance and core design coursework.

Fuel pellet fabrication, cladding materials, and the fuel-cladding chemical interactions that develop over a fuel rod's life are the technical core of this course. Students track fuel performance through burnup, fission gas release, and dimensional changes, and evaluate fuel cycle chemistry for both uranium oxide and advanced fuel forms. The course connects fuel behavior to the operating limits imposed on reactor cores.

Fuel assembly geometry, enrichment distribution, and control rod placement are examined as design variables that determine a reactor core's neutron economy and power distribution. Students calculate power peaking factors and thermal margins against safety limits, and evaluate how core loading patterns affect fuel cycle length across successive fuel cycles. The course develops the design tradeoffs that core designers balance when planning a reactor's operating life.

Physical principles behind gamma camera, computed tomography, and positron emission imaging are developed from the interaction of radiation with detector and tissue material. Students trace the path from photon emission through detection to reconstructed image, comparing spatial resolution and sensitivity tradeoffs across modalities. The course sets up the physics used in later imaging and medical physics coursework.

Ionized gases are described through single-particle motion in electric and magnetic fields, then through fluid and kinetic models that predict collective behavior such as Debye shielding, plasma oscillations, and wave propagation. Diagnostic techniques used to measure plasma parameters, including probes and spectroscopic methods, are covered alongside the theory they are meant to test. Applications span fusion confinement concepts, plasma processing, and space plasma phenomena. Cross-listed with EENG-4080.

Working with a small laboratory plasma source, students measure electron temperature and density using electrostatic probes and observe basic plasma phenomena such as sheath formation and wave propagation. Diagnostic techniques including optical emission spectroscopy are used to characterize discharge conditions, and results are compared to the theoretical models covered in lecture. Laboratory companion to NUCL-3055. Cross-listed with EENG-4085.

Senior Design I opens the capstone sequence with team-based conceptual design of a nuclear or radiological engineering system chosen in consultation with the department. Students define design requirements, evaluate competing concepts against safety and performance criteria, and produce a preliminary design package supported by engineering calculations. Project scheduling and design reviews are practiced alongside the technical work. The course ends with a formal preliminary design review presented to a faculty panel.

Senior Design II carries the project defined in the first design course through detailed design, analysis, and final documentation. Students refine their design in response to preliminary review feedback, complete supporting calculations and safety arguments, and produce a final design report and drawing package. Teams present and defend their completed design in a format resembling professional design review. The course closes out the design sequence and the undergraduate degree program.

Neutron transport and reactor physics develops the diffusion and transport equations that govern the steady-state neutron population in a reactor core. Students compute multiplication factors, flux distributions, and criticality conditions for multi-region core geometries, and compare diffusion-theory results against transport-theory benchmarks. Multigroup energy treatment and simple numerical solution methods are used to connect the underlying physics to practical core calculations. The course extends the kinetics behavior studied earlier into a full steady-state physics treatment.

Commercial reactor types, including pressurized water, boiling water, and advanced designs, are compared for their core configuration, coolant system, and safety systems. Students analyze plant-level thermodynamic cycles, balance of plant systems, and the operational characteristics that distinguish each reactor type. The course connects reactor physics and thermal-hydraulics concepts to full power plant design and operation.

course_title: Computational Fluid Dynamics for Nuclear Applications
course_desc: Mesh generation and discretization of the governing flow equations introduce students to computational fluid dynamics as applied to nuclear reactor components such as coolant channels and fuel assemblies. Students set up and run simulations using standard turbulence models, then compare predicted velocity and temperature fields against benchmark data. The course emphasizes correct problem setup and result verification over the underlying numerical theory.

Magnetic confinement concepts, including the tokamak and stellarator configurations, are examined alongside the engineering challenges of sustaining a burning plasma. Students study first-wall and blanket materials, tritium breeding, and the heat removal systems required to handle fusion power densities. The course addresses the specific engineering problems that separate fusion reactor design from fission reactor practice.

Kinetic theory of plasmas extends the fluid-like descriptions used in introductory treatments, developing the Vlasov equation and its role in describing collisionless plasma behavior. Students analyze plasma waves, instabilities, and Landau damping, then apply the theory to confinement and heating problems relevant to fusion devices. The course moves quickly into advanced kinetic and wave phenomena built on a working knowledge of basic plasma concepts.

Attenuation and buildup factor calculations for gamma rays and neutrons form the quantitative core of this course, applied to shield design for reactors, medical facilities, and radioactive material storage. Students select shielding materials and thicknesses to meet dose limits at specified distances, accounting for source geometry and scattered radiation. The course culminates in a shielding design project evaluated against regulatory dose criteria.

Radiation protection principles are applied specifically to medical settings in this course, covering dose limits for patients, staff, and the public in diagnostic and therapeutic environments. Students design shielding and room layouts for imaging suites and treatment areas, and evaluate regulatory compliance requirements for medical radiation facilities. Case studies address quality assurance programs and incident reporting practices in clinical radiation use.

Advanced dosimetry calculations, including cavity theory and dose conversion coefficients, extend the measurement and shielding concepts developed earlier in the curriculum. Students compute absorbed, equivalent, and effective dose for complex exposure scenarios and evaluate dosimeter response across radiation types and energies. This course draws together radiological physics principles from across the nuclear engineering sequence.

Treatment planning for external beam and brachytherapy is developed from the physics of linear accelerators and sealed radioactive sources used in cancer therapy. Students calculate dose distributions using treatment planning algorithms and evaluate plan quality against target coverage and organ-at-risk constraints. Quality assurance procedures for therapy equipment round out the course's clinical physics content.

course_title: Research in Nuclear Engineering and Radiological Sciences
course_desc: Students undertake a supervised research project in nuclear engineering or radiological sciences under a faculty advisor's direction, beginning with a written proposal defining scope and methods. Work proceeds through data collection or analysis appropriate to the chosen topic, culminating in a written report and a presentation of findings to the sponsoring research group. The course structure varies by project but consistently requires a proposal, a final report, and a presentation.
